In 2004, a study published in a prominent Cambridge-based archaeology journal unveiled a major discovery in Somerset, England. Employing high-sensitivity magnetic mapping, researchers brought to light a substantial, formerly unrecognized Neolithic henge monument, inviting comparisons to England's most famous prehistoric stone circle in Wiltshire. 

A key contributor to this Somerset investigation had previously, in the mid-1990s and within the same journal, reported on new features within another significant Wiltshire henge complex, identified through a combination of aerial observation during dry conditions and ground-based sensing techniques, collaborating with specialists from England's national monument laboratories. Personnel associated with national heritage efforts and a northern English university were also involved in the later 2004 Somerset project, highlighting the evolution of non-destructive methods for archaeological discovery.

What is the exact title of the 2004 paper suggesting a new challenger to the Wiltshire giant's status?
label: A Rival to Stonehenge? Geophysical Survey at Stanton Drew, England

Published in an international review bridging these two fields, the work examined why certain legal frameworks, such as sales laws echoing American codes, gain global traction. It proposed that this phenomenon is less about intrinsic preference and more akin to a coordination problem swayed by economic influence. What is the precise title of this investigation into aligning disparate systems across borders?
label: Harmonization of Private Law on a Global Level
